title: Levers: force times distance
summary: Build a lever from a ruler and a fulcrum, measure the lifting force with a spring scale at three arm lengths, and find the trade a lever always makes.
materials: stiff wooden ruler or a wooden dowel about 30 cm long
pencil or a small triangular block, for the fulcrum
a bag of washers or coins as a fixed load
tape measure or ruler for marking arm lengths
string and a second spool or pencil, for the pulley extra

figure.alt: A ruler-lever rests on a triangular fulcrum in the middle. The load hangs on the left at a fixed distance from the fulcrum, and three marks are drawn on the right side of the bar at 8, 16 and 24 centimetres from the fulcrum, where the spring scale will pull down to lift the load.

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop starts the season: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: can a small push lift a big load? A person cannot always pull as hard as a job needs, but a machine can trade one thing for another to make a push do more. This week's machine is the oldest one there is: the lever.

Imagine: a stiff bar resting on a fixed point, the fulcrum. Push down on one side and the other side lifts. Move where you push and the same push does something different.

Plan: sketch the lever on graph paper before building it. Draw the fulcrum in the middle, the load on one side at a fixed distance, and three marks on the effort side at three different distances from the fulcrum. Label each mark with its distance in centimetres. You will hook the spring scale at each mark in turn and pull until the load just lifts.

figure.alt: A lever bar balances on a fulcrum in the middle. The load sits ten centimetres to the left. Pushing down at ten centimetres on the right needs six newtons, but pushing down further out at thirty centimetres on the right only needs two newtons to lift the same load.

steps.title: A lever trades distance for force
steps.body:
A lever is a stiff bar that turns around one fixed point, the fulcrum. Push down on one side and the other side pushes up, and how hard the push needs to be depends on how far it sits from the fulcrum.

The rule is a balance: force times distance from the fulcrum is the same on both sides. If a load sits 10 centimetres from the fulcrum, it takes 6 newtons of force to lift by pushing right beside it. Moving the push out to 30 centimetres away only takes 2 newtons, a third as much. That is because the distance became three times as long.

A lever never makes force appear from nowhere. It trades distance for force: a longer effort arm needs less force, but your hand has to travel further to lift the load the same height. Gears make the same trade with turns instead of a straight push, and the trade shows up again next week.

figure.alt: The ruler rests as a lever on a triangular fulcrum. A bag of washers hangs eight centimetres to the left of the fulcrum. The spring scale hooks onto the ruler on the right side, shown here at the twenty-four centimetre mark, and pulls straight down to lift the load.

steps.title: Build the lever and measure three arm lengths
steps.body:
Rest the ruler on the fulcrum so it balances close to level with nothing hanging on it, and mark that balance point. Hook the bag of washers to one end at a fixed distance from the fulcrum, say 8 centimetres, and leave that distance the same for the whole test. That is the load arm, and it does not change today.

On the other side, mark three effort distances from the fulcrum: for example 8, 16 and 24 centimetres. At each mark, hook the spring scale, pull down slowly and read the force the instant the load just lifts off the table. Write each reading on your graph paper sketch next to its mark.

Pull smoothly, not with a jerk, since a sudden yank reads higher than the true lifting force. Read each length three times and use the middle (median) of the three readings, since your own pulling wobbles a little each time.
checklist: The lever balances close to level on the fulcrum before any load is added
The load and its distance from the fulcrum stayed exactly the same for all three tests
Three effort arm lengths were tested, each pulled slowly and read three times
The readings drop as the effort arm gets longer, matching the science step

steps.title: Arm length versus force
steps.body:
Only the effort arm length changes between rows. The load and its distance from the fulcrum stay exactly the same for all nine rows, and so does the fulcrum's position.

Test three effort arm lengths, three runs each, nine rows in total. For each run, pull the spring scale slowly and write down the force in newtons the instant the load lifts off the table.
steps.question: Which effort arm length needed the least force, and about how many newtons less was it than the shortest arm?

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body: One line for each thing that did not work the first time and what you tried. Classics this week: the fulcrum sliding out from under the ruler mid-pull, and a jerky pull that reads too high. Also watch for the load arm accidentally moving between tests, which breaks the fair comparison and means starting that column again.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo of the lever set up on the fulcrum with the spring scale hooked at its longest mark, next to your graph paper sketch with all nine readings written on it

extras.title: The pulley: force redirected, or force cut in half
extras.body:
1. Loop a string over a fixed spool or a pencil held steady above the load, so pulling the string down lifts the load straight up. Measure the pull force with the spring scale.

2. Compare it with the force needed to lift the same load straight up with no pulley at all, spring scale hooked directly to the load.

3. Now hang the load from a second, moving spool, run the string up over the fixed spool and back down to your hand, and lift again. Measure the pull force this way too.

4. Write all three forces side by side in the Maker's Log: direct lift, one fixed pulley, one moving pulley.

Notice that a single fixed pulley only changes the direction of your pull, not the amount of force. Adding the moving pulley should roughly halve the force, the same trade a longer lever arm makes.
